_source: Live Sound KB mic-library.md (character/EQ + use cases) + manufacturer published specifications. Generated pages via mic_page_gen.py. See NEW-MIC-WORKFLOW.md.
_note: owned:false = reference/EQ page only, not in the locker (faded gallery ring). Existing hand-built pages (audio-technica-pro-6l, dpa-4099) are listed for the gallery but must NOT be regenerated — build new mics with --slug, then run mic_wire.py once.

mics.name: Shure SM57
mics.description: Cardioid dynamic — the industry-standard snare and guitar-cab workhorse.
mics.summary: The reference instrument dynamic: mid-forward, tough, and predictable. Primary snare top and guitar cab, utility anywhere.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (SM57); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The mic every input list falls back on. A cardioid dynamic with a forward 3–5 kHz presence hump, tight low end, and enough SPL handling to sit in front of anything. It builds box and honk in the 300–500 Hz range on close sources, which is the one move it almost always needs — otherwise it takes EQ cleanly and behaves the same night after night.
mics.sound: Mid-forward and proximity-prone, with a presence lift through 3–5 kHz that cuts snare and amp grit through a mix. Thin below ~100 Hz, so it stays out of the way of the kick. On cabs and snare it builds 300–500 Hz box — find and cut that first.
bestfit: Snare top — the default; ~1 in over the rim angled at the center, tame ~400 Hz box.
Guitar cab — on-axis to the dust cap for bite, edge of cone for warmth; pair with an R-121 for the AxeMount blend at Memo.
Utility — horns, perc, anything loud that needs a rugged, honest mic.
notes: Proximity-prone — back off or HPF if it gets chesty up close.
AxeMount blend at Memo: SM57 primary (CH13) + R-121 (CH15), ribbon 6–10 dB under. Sum in mono and polarity-check.
Cut box ~400 Hz before boosting anything.
comparable: Step up for toms and low-mid girth on cabs
More open, more body, slightly scooped mids

mics.name: Shure SM58
mics.description: Cardioid dynamic vocal mic — the handheld standard for typical gigs.
mics.summary: The SM57 capsule behind a ball grille and pop filter. Consistent, roadproof handheld vocal for the everyday show.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (SM58); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The default handheld. Same essential capsule as the 57 with a built-in pop filter and a gentle low rolloff to tame proximity. A ~4–6 kHz presence lift gives vocals cut without hype. It's muddy if eaten and short on air up top, but it's tough, feedback-resistant, and utterly predictable.
mics.sound: Warm, midrange-centered, with a presence rise ~4–6 kHz and a controlled low end. Proximity gives it body up close; back off for a more even tone. Cut box around 500 Hz if it piles up.
bestfit: Lead and backing vocals — typical gigs where you want zero surprises.
Spoken word / MC — rugged and forgiving of technique.
Utility handheld — the one you hand anyone.
notes: Muddy if the singer eats it — coach distance or add a small HPF.
Limited air above ~12 kHz; reach for a KMS 105 when you want detail.
comparable: Stage condenser step-up for detail and air

mics.name: Shure Beta 58A
mics.description: Supercardioid dynamic vocal — brighter and tighter than an SM58 for loud stages.
mics.summary: Supercardioid vocal dynamic with more bite, more air, and more gain-before-feedback than a 58. The loud-stage handheld.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (Beta 58A); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: When the stage is loud and rejection matters, this is the handheld. A tighter supercardioid pattern with two presence peaks — around 4 kHz and again near 10 kHz — makes it brighter and more cutting than an SM58, with more gain-before-feedback. Those same peaks can turn strident or sibilant on a bright voice, so it wants a little presence restraint.
mics.sound: Brighter and more forward than a 58 with a tighter null. The low end is attenuated below ~500 Hz for proximity control. Ease off the presence peaks and tame ~600 Hz box on close, chesty voices.
bestfit: Lead vocals on loud stages — better rejection, more cut.
Aggressive/rock vocals that need to slice through.
Any spot fighting monitor bleed where the tight null helps.
notes: Supercardioid rejects at the sides, nulls at ~126° — aim wedges into the rear null, not straight behind.
Watch sibilance from the ~10 kHz peak — a gentle de-ess or shelf tame helps.
comparable: Warmer, less bright, wider cardioid pattern
Condenser detail with a smoother top

mics.name: Shure Beta 52A
mics.description: Tailored supercardioid kick dynamic — scooped low-mids, big lows, voiced click.
mics.summary: Purpose-built kick mic with the thump and beater click baked in. Body layer inside the drum; pairs with a Beta 91A on the head.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (Beta 52A); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A kick specialist voiced so you barely have to touch it: deep lows, a scooped low-mid to clear the mud, and a presence lift around 4 kHz for beater click. High SPL handling and an integral stand mount make it a fast, roadproof inside-the-drum body mic.
mics.sound: Big, scooped kick voicing — thump plus click with a hole in the low-mids. Ease off the built-in scoop rather than adding to it; if you want more knock, nudge 3–4 kHz, and clear any box around 300–400 Hz.
bestfit: Kick — body/thump layer inside the drum, aimed at the beater zone.
Two-mic kick — pair with a Beta 91A boundary on the head for click; blend and EQ differently.
Floor tom or large low sources in a pinch.
notes: The voicing is aggressive out of the box — subtractive tweaks beat piling on more.
Standard two-mic kick at Memo: Beta 52A + Beta 91A.
comparable: Similar scooped kick voicing, a touch clickier
Boundary partner for the head/click layer

mics.name: Audix D6
mics.description: Pre-scooped cardioid kick dynamic — thump and click baked in, needs almost no EQ.
mics.summary: The 'smiley-curve' kick mic: peaks around 63 Hz and 5 kHz with a deep mid scoop. Attack and click layer; plug in and go.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (D6); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A one-trick mic that does its one trick perfectly. The D6 is voiced with a big low peak near 63 Hz, a deep scoop around 600 Hz, and a presence spike near 5 kHz — modern kick, no EQ required. It has essentially no midrange body, which is exactly the point when you pair it or want click-forward attack.
mics.sound: Scooped, hyped, modern — thump plus click with the mids carved out. Ease off attack, boom, box and mud since they're already dialed; it needs almost nothing.
bestfit: Kick — attack/click layer inside; the 'sounds finished' kick mic.
Pair with a Beta 52A or DM6 when you want more body underneath.
Floor tom for a punchy, scooped low tom.
notes: No mid body by design — don't try to EQ warmth back in, layer a body mic instead.
Fast to deploy: often usable flat.
comparable: Similar scooped kick, slightly less click-forward
Flat, honest kick condenser — the opposite philosophy

mics.name: Audix i5
mics.description: Cardioid dynamic instrument mic — a more open, fuller-bodied SM57 alternative.
mics.summary: Punchy cardioid instrument dynamic with more body and a more open top than a 57. Snare, cabs, brass.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (i5); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: Audix's answer to the 57, and a good one. A body lift around 150 Hz and a presence peak near 5.5 kHz give it more weight and a more open sound than a 57, with slightly less scooped mids. That 5.5 kHz peak can get harsh on a cracky snare, so it's the move to watch.
mics.sound: Fuller and more open than a 57, with real body and a forward presence peak. Ease off body, crack and snap; tame the harsh ~5.5 kHz if the snare cracks hard.
bestfit: Snare top — when you want more body than a 57.
Guitar cab — punchy and open.
Brass and perc utility.
notes: Watch the 5.5 kHz peak on bright/cracky snares.
Rugged VLM capsule — fast recovery, high SPL.
comparable: The reference — i5 is fuller and more open

mics.name: Audix D2
mics.description: Hypercardioid dynamic tom mic — punchy and articulate on rack toms.
mics.summary: Rack-tom hypercardioid with a 150 Hz body bump and articulate upper mids. Punchy, tight rejection, part of the DP8 pack.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (D2); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The mid-tom of the D-series. A hypercardioid with a lift around 150 Hz, a dip through 500 Hz–1 kHz, and a subtle upper-mid rise — punchy and articulate with tight off-axis rejection. Leaner in the deep lows than a D4, which is exactly right for rack toms.
mics.sound: Punchy and articulate with a defined attack. Ease off boom and mud; it's already voiced for tom clarity.
bestfit: Rack / small-mid toms — the D-series default.
Congas and hand perc where the tight pattern helps.
notes: Hypercardioid — mind the rear lobe when placing near cymbals.
Leaner lows than a D4; use D4 on the floor tom.
comparable: More low-end extension for the floor tom
Bigger, more girth — the standalone tom step-up

mics.name: Audix D4
mics.description: Hypercardioid dynamic for low sources — deep, resonant floor toms.
mics.summary: Low-source hypercardioid reaching down to ~35 Hz with a smooth low-mid. Deep and resonant on floor toms and low percussion.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (D4); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The floor-tom and low-source member of the D-series. Nearly flat to ~63 Hz with a rise near 80 Hz and reach down toward 35 Hz, plus a smooth (not scooped) 800 Hz–1 kHz. Deep and resonant, with a little less upper-mid attack than a D2 — so it may want a touch of click.
mics.sound: Deep and full with a natural low-mid. Ease off boom and mud; add a touch of upper-mid attack if the tom needs more stick.
bestfit: Floor toms — the D-series low mic.
Low congas, cajon, djembe and similar low percussion.
notes: More low reach than a D2 — keep it on the floor tom.
May want a small attack lift where the D2 doesn't.

mics.name: sE V-Kick
mics.description: Compact supercardioid kick dynamic with four voicing settings.
mics.summary: sE's kick mic from the V Pack Arena — dynamic supercardioid reaching to 20 Hz, with switchable voicings and an adjustable swivel mount.
mics.sources: sE Electronics published specifications (V Kick); thomannmusic.com; Live Sound KB mic-library notes
mics.intro: The kick mic in the V Pack Arena kit. A compact dynamic supercardioid that reaches down to 20 Hz, with four selectable sound settings so you can dial the balance of thump and click at the mic and an adjustable swivel mount for precise placement inside the drum.
mics.sound: Modern kick voicing with the tone shaped at the mic via the four settings. Start from the setting closest to the sound you want, then trim rather than fight it on the desk.
bestfit: Kick — compact dynamic alternative, easy to place inside the drum.
Situations where the swivel mount and voicings speed up setup.
notes: Pick the voicing setting first, then EQ.
Part of the sE V Pack Arena drum kit.

mics.name: sE V-Beat
mics.description: Clip-mount supercardioid tom dynamic from the V Pack Arena.
mics.summary: Dynamic supercardioid tom mic on a clamp mount — shares the V7 X capsule voicing. Fast to rig, tight rejection.
mics.sources: sE Electronics published specifications (V Beat); thomannmusic.com; Live Sound KB mic-library notes
mics.intro: The tom mic of the V Pack Arena, on a clip/clamp mount for quick rigging on the rim. It shares its capsule and response with the V7 X — a supercardioid with a full range up to 19 kHz and tight off-axis rejection, so it isolates well in a busy kit.
mics.sound: Full-range and articulate with tight rejection — the same voicing as the V7 X. Shape toms as usual; the tight pattern keeps cymbal bleed down.
bestfit: Rack and floor toms — clip-mounted, fast setup.
Busy kits where isolation matters.
notes: Same capsule as the V7 X — expect matched tone across the kit.
Part of the sE V Pack Arena drum kit.

mics.name: sE V7 X
mics.description: Supercardioid dynamic instrument mic — snare and cab, with an aluminium voice coil.
mics.summary: The instrument version of sE's V7. Supercardioid dynamic with an aluminium voice coil for detail, wide 30 Hz–19 kHz response. Snare, cabs, perc.
mics.sources: sE Electronics published specifications (V7 X); thomannmusic.com; Live Sound KB mic-library notes
mics.intro: An instrument-voiced supercardioid dynamic with an aluminium voice coil for extra top-end detail. Wide response to 19 kHz and a tight pattern make it a capable snare and cab mic — a modern alternative to a 57 with a little more openness and reach.
mics.sound: Detailed and open for a dynamic, with a tight supercardioid null. Shape like a 57 but expect a bit more air; watch presence on bright sources.
bestfit: Snare top — supercardioid rejection helps on loud stages.
Guitar cab and general amplified-instrument duty.
Percussion utility.
notes: Shares its capsule with the V-Beat tom mic.
Tight null — aim it to reject the nearest bleed source.
comparable: The reference — V7 X is more open up top

mics.name: Sennheiser MD 421-U (Silver Tail)
mics.description: Vintage 1970s MD 421-U 'Silver Tail' — the XLR large-diaphragm cardioid dynamic with the chrome connector base. Toms, brass, cabs; 5-position bass rolloff.
mics.summary: Brian's are the 1970s MD 421-U — the 'Silver Tail': black body, native XLR, and the chrome/silver connector base that names it. One generation on from the cream Delrin originals and distinct from the all-black 90s -U and the 2002 MD 421-II. Same legendary 421 element.
mics.sources: Wikipedia — Sennheiser MD 421 (version history); Sennheiser MD 421 heritage; owner identification (Brian Lloyd — 1970s Silver Tail U-series); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: Not the modern MD 421-II — these are the vintage 1970s **MD 421-U**, the ones collectors call the 'Silver Tail' for the chrome connector base at the butt of the mic. The -U was the first 421 to run a native XLR output (the earlier -2, -N and -HL used the small Tuchel/DIN connector, so no adapter here), and it sits a generation on from the light cream Delrin originals but before the all-black 90s bodies and the economical 2002 MD 421-II. Same 27 mm large-diaphragm element that has run essentially unchanged since 1960 — a genuinely different vintage from the black II, which is Brian's point.

specs.Stand clip: MZA quick-release (U5 = fixed 3/8" US thread; U4 = interchangeable)
specs.Status: Vintage — discontinued; element continues in the MD 421-II

mics.sound: The classic 421 voice: near-linear lows up to ~1 kHz, real low-mid girth, and a smooth upper-mid presence rise — 'an SM57 on steroids.' That low-mid can bloat 200–400 Hz up close; pull the M–S rotary toward S or notch ~300 Hz. Ease off boom and presence to taste.
bestfit: Toms — first choice, rack and floor.
Brass — trombone, sax, trumpet section.
Guitar cabs — pairs with a 57 for low-mid weight (watch the 200–400 Hz stack).
notes: These are the 1970s 'Silver Tail' MD 421-U — chrome connector base, native XLR — NOT the all-black 90s -U or the 2002 MD 421-II. The element is the same lineage; the vintage build is prized.
No Tuchel adapter needed — the -U is already XLR (unlike the -2 / -N / -HL).
Use the M–S bass rolloff before reaching for the desk HPF.
The MZA quick-release clip is notorious for dropping the mic — seat it fully (a zip tie on the latch is the classic fix).
comparable: The 2002 all-black production version — same element, economical build
Smaller, thinner — the 421 adds girth and weight

mics.name: Sennheiser e609 Silver
mics.description: Flat side-address supercardioid dynamic — hang it over a guitar cab.
mics.summary: Side-address cab dynamic you drape over the grille — no stand needed. Bright upper-mid presence, supercardioid rejection.
mics.sources: Sennheiser published specifications (e609 Silver); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A flat-faced, side-address dynamic built to hang over the front of a guitar cab by its own cable — no stand, no fuss. A bright upper-mid/presence lift around 4–5 kHz and a supercardioid pattern give it cut and isolation, though it can get edgy on already-bright amps.
mics.sound: Bright and forward through the upper mids, supercardioid tight. Ease off presence and tame ~2.8 kHz edge on bright cabs; position over the cone edge for less fizz.
bestfit: Guitar cab — draped over the grille, fast to deploy.
Any spot where you want a stand-free cab mic.
notes: Position over the grille changes tone a lot — cone edge = warmer, dust cap = brighter.
Can get edgy on bright amps; blend with a ribbon if needed.
comparable: Ribbon blend partner to tame brightness

mics.name: Sennheiser e604
mics.description: Clip-on cardioid dynamic for toms — fast setup, voiced attack.
mics.summary: Lightweight clip-on tom dynamic with scooped low-mids and a voiced attack. Quick to rig, thinner than a D-series.
mics.sources: Sennheiser published specifications (e604); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A small clip-on cardioid dynamic built for fast tom setups — it clamps to the rim and stays out of the drummer's way. Scooped low-mids and a voiced attack give it punch, though it's thinner and a touch boxier than a stand-mounted D-series and modest in the deep lows.
mics.sound: Punchy and quick with scooped low-mids. Ease off attack and mud; add low-end body if the tom sounds thin.
bestfit: Toms — clip-on, quick setup, tidy stage.
Fast changeovers and festival kits.
notes: Thinner/boxier than a D-series — worth it for the speed.
Modest deep lows; the D4 wins on a big floor tom.

mics.name: Shure Beta 27
mics.description: Supercardioid large-diaphragm condenser — open, clean, flatter than a 57 on cabs and instruments.
mics.summary: Side-address supercardioid LDC. Flat through the low-mids with small, tasteful presence peaks — an open, clean alternative to a dynamic on cabs, brass and acoustic sources.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (Beta 27); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A side-address supercardioid condenser that trades a dynamic's color for openness. Essentially flat from 60 Hz to 3 kHz with small +2 dB peaks near 5.5 kHz and 9 kHz — flatter and cleaner than a 57 — plus a −15 dB pad for loud sources. The one thing to watch is a little 9 kHz fizz on already-bright amps.
mics.sound: Open and clean with an honest low-mid and gentle presence. Ease off box and honk; tame the ~9 kHz fizz on bright cabs. Engage the pad on loud amps and the HPF on close, boomy sources.
bestfit: Guitar cab — a cleaner, flatter alternative to a 57; pairs well with one.
Brass and acoustic instruments needing detail without hype.
Loud percussion and utility instrument duty (use the pad).
notes: Needs 48 V phantom — it's a condenser, unlike the dynamics it often sits beside.
Blends nicely with an SM57 on a cab (57 grit + Beta 27 clean body/air).
comparable: The dynamic reference — Beta 27 is flatter and more open

mics.name: Schoeps CMC6 + MK4
mics.description: Reference cardioid SDC (CMC6 amp + MK4 capsule) — the classical spot/main standard.
mics.summary: The reference small-diaphragm cardioid: transparent, flat with a gentle ~10 kHz rise that compensates room HF loss. Classical spots and mains.
mics.sources: Schoeps published specifications (CMC6 / MK4); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The Colette-system workhorse: a CMC6 amplifier body with an MK4 cardioid capsule. Ruler-flat and transparent with a slight ~10 kHz lift that quietly compensates for a room's high-frequency loss, a constant polar pattern, and a natural, uncolored sound. It's the classical spot and main-pair reference — pricey and fragile, but honest.
mics.sound: Transparent and natural with a whisper of top-end air. Barely needs EQ; ease off presence only if a bright room over-airs it. Subtractive, minimal — this is a classical blend mic.
bestfit: Classical spots — soloists, sections, close detail.
Main pair — ORTF/NOS on the Memo wire array.
Acoustic instruments needing an honest, uncolored capture.
notes: Fragile and expensive — handle and store with care.
Capsule swaps: MK5 (omni/cardioid), MK41 (supercardioid) share the CMC6 body.

mics.name: Schoeps CMC6 + MK5
mics.description: Switchable omni/cardioid SDC (CMC6 + MK5) — classical room, Decca tree, wide ambient.
mics.summary: CMC6 body with the MK5 capsule: switchable omni/cardioid, both patterns carrying an HF lift (brighter than an MK4). Omni mode is natural with extended lows.
mics.sources: Schoeps published specifications (CMC6 / MK5); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The flexible member of the set: an MK5 capsule that switches between omni and cardioid. Both patterns carry a slight HF lift — a touch brighter than an MK4 — and the omni mode is beautifully natural with extended low end. First call for room, Decca-tree, and wide ambient on classical dates.
mics.sound: Natural with an airy top; omni mode adds warmth and low extension. That top lift can over-air a bright room — ease off presence/air if needed.
bestfit: Classical main pair / room — omni for warmth and width.
Decca tree center and flanks.
Wide ambient capture where the MK4 would be too tight.
notes: Switch pattern at the capsule; omni for reverberant halls, cardioid for tighter blend.
Preferred main pair on the Memo wire array (cardioid ORTF; omni for more warmth).

mics.name: Schoeps CMC6 + MK41
mics.description: Supercardioid SDC (CMC6 + MK41) — tight classical spot with strong rejection.
mics.summary: CMC6 body with the MK41 supercardioid capsule: tight, natural, with gentle presence and excellent off-axis rejection. Classical spot where isolation matters.
mics.sources: Schoeps published specifications (CMC6 / MK41); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The tight one. An MK41 supercardioid capsule on the CMC6 body — natural with a gentle presence rise and the strong rejection you want when a spot has to stay out of its neighbors. Slight off-axis coloration at extreme angles is the only trade against an MK4.
mics.sound: Tight and natural with a light presence lift. Minimal EQ; ease off presence only if needed. The supercardioid null is the tool — aim it at the bleed.
bestfit: Classical spot mics needing tight isolation.
Soloist coverage in a busy stage.
Sections where an MK4's wider pattern picks up too much neighbor.
notes: Watch extreme off-axis coloration when aiming the null.
Shares the CMC6 body with the MK4 and MK5 capsules.

mics.name: Sennheiser MKH 40
mics.description: RF-condenser cardioid — pristine, extremely low noise. Classical main pair, flute, detail.
mics.summary: The low-noise classical main-pair mic. RF-bias cardioid, near-flat with a slight airy presence, and one of the quietest capsules made.
mics.sources: Sennheiser published specifications (MKH 40); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: An RF-bias condenser that stays quiet where others hiss. Near-flat with a slight airy presence, extremely low self-noise, and pristine detail on flute, strings and classical mains. It's clinical and can bloom on proximity, which is exactly why it flatters a well-placed main pair.
mics.sound: Clean, quiet, airy. Ease off presence only if it gets clinical; otherwise let it be — it's a blend/main mic, not a shaping tool.
bestfit: Classical main pair — ORTF, NOS, spaced omni arrays.
Flute and woodwind detail (Brian's go-to).
Any quiet, high-detail acoustic capture.
notes: The low self-noise is the whole point on quiet passages.
Proximity if placed close — back off for the natural tone.

mics.name: Shure SM81
mics.description: Ruler-flat cardioid SDC — hat, overheads, acoustic. Takes EQ cleanly.
mics.summary: The clean, flat SDC standard. Detailed highs with no harsh fizz and a switchable HPF; accurate on hat, overheads and acoustic instruments.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (SM81); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A flat, honest cardioid condenser with clean, detailed highs and no built-in flattery. Switchable HPF (flat / 6 / 18 dB/oct) and a wide, even response make it accurate on hi-hat, overheads and acoustic instruments — it takes EQ cleanly and reveals a source honestly, so it needs care on cymbal wash.
mics.sound: Flat and detailed — apply the template as-is. Watch cymbal wash and sibilance since nothing is hyped; use the HPF on close acoustic sources.
bestfit: Hi-hat — clean and detailed.
Overheads — accurate, honest cymbals.
Acoustic guitar and instruments — takes EQ well.
notes: Use the onboard HPF before the desk filter.
No hype — flatters nothing, which is the point.

mics.name: Shure Beta 91A
mics.description: Half-cardioid boundary condenser — kick attack layer, piano. Contour switch.
mics.summary: Boundary condenser for kick (on the head, inside) and piano. Solid boundary lows plus pronounced beater click; a contour switch tames shell boxiness.
mics.sources: Shure published specifications (Beta 91A); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A half-cardioid boundary condenser built to lie inside the kick on the resonant head. Solid boundary low end plus a pronounced beater click, nominally flat with a contour switch that cuts ~7 dB at 400 Hz to clear shell boxiness. Standard partner to a Beta 52A for a two-mic kick.
mics.sound: Boundary lows plus click; picks up shell box ~300–500 Hz — engage the contour or notch. Ease off boom to taste.
bestfit: Kick — attack/click layer inside on the resonant head; pair with a Beta 52A.
Piano — boundary under the lid.
Low boundary pickup where a stand mic won't fit.
notes: Standard two-mic kick at Memo: Beta 52A (body) + Beta 91A (click).
Contour switch first, desk EQ second.
comparable: Body/thump partner for the two-mic kick

mics.name: Audix M1280B
mics.description: Miniature cardioid condenser with integrated preamp — overheads, cymbals, ensemble.
mics.summary: Compact cardioid condenser, RF-immune with an integrated preamp and generous front pickup. Overheads, cymbals and ensemble — thin lows, room-sensitive.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (M1280B); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: A miniaturized cardioid condenser with a fully integrated preamp and complete RF immunity — no phantom-hungry electronics dangling on the stand. Extended response and a generous front pickup make it a tidy overhead and ensemble mic; the lows are thin and it's room-sensitive, so placement matters.
mics.sound: Clean with a slightly forward presence — ease off presence. Thin lows; HPF and lean on placement to control room.
bestfit: Overheads / cymbals — matched pair, compact.
Ensemble and choral pickup.
Tight spaces where a full SDC won't fit.
notes: RF-immune — safe near wireless and phones.
Part of the Audix DP8 pack.

mics.name: Audix M1280BHC
mics.description: Miniature hypercardioid condenser — hi-hat, tight overhead, podium.
mics.summary: Hypercardioid version of the M1280 — extended response, integrated preamp, RF-immune, tight isolation. Hi-hat and tight overhead duty.
mics.sources: Audix published specifications (M1280BHC); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: The hypercardioid M1280 — same compact, RF-immune, integrated-preamp build with a tighter pattern for isolation. Ideal on hi-hat and as a tight overhead or podium mic; the lows are thin and the upper mids run a touch forward.
mics.sound: Tight and clean with forward upper mids — ease off presence. Thin lows; the tight pattern keeps bleed down.
bestfit: Hi-hat — tight isolation from snare/cymbals.
Tight overhead or spot.
Podium/lectern where rejection matters.
notes: Hypercardioid — mind the rear lobe.
Part of the Audix DP8 pack.

mics.name: Earthworks DM6
mics.description: SeisMic flat/extended-LF kick condenser — honest, huge sub reach, takes full shaping.
mics.summary: An uncolored, extended-low-frequency kick condenser with fast transients. Captures everything honestly, so it takes full EQ shaping to a modern kick.
mics.sources: Earthworks published specifications (DM6); Live Sound KB mic-library character notes
mics.intro: Earthworks' honest kick mic. A flat, extended-low-frequency condenser with fast transient response and huge sub reach — the opposite of a pre-scooped kick mic. It captures the drum truthfully (including bleed), which means it takes full EQ shaping to whatever modern kick you want.
mics.sound: Flat and honest — apply the template fully; it needs EQ to get a 'modern' kick. Captures everything, so mind bleed.
bestfit: Kick — inside, when you want to shape from a true source.
Low percussion needing honest sub reach.
Pair with a scooped dynamic for blend.
notes: Part of the Earthworks DK-6 kit.
Uncolored — flatters nothing; the shaping is yours.

mics.name: Earthworks DM17

mics.intro: Telefunken's class-A FET pencil condenser — hand-built with an American transformer and an ultra-quiet 5 dB A self-noise. The TK60 cardioid capsule is flat from 150 Hz to 7 kHz with a smooth, airy presence peak at 8 kHz; interchangeable capsules cover omni and hypercardioid. Fast, detailed, and happy at very high SPL — a premium alternative to an SM81 on acoustic sources, overheads and brass.

specs.Type: Condenser (small diaphragm, class-A FET, interchangeable capsule)
specs.Frequency response: 20 Hz – 20 kHz (±3 dB); circuit linear ±2 dB 20 Hz–50 kHz

mics.sound: Fast, detailed, airy — ease off presence/air if a bright room over-airs the 8 kHz peak. Very quiet, so it flatters soft acoustic passages.
bestfit: Acoustic guitar and instruments — detailed, airy.
Drum overheads and cymbals (very high SPL headroom).
Brass and woodwind spot; classical detail.
notes: Ultra-low self-noise (5 dB A) — excellent on quiet sources.
Interchangeable capsules: TK60 cardioid (default), plus omni/hyper.
Premium step up from an SM81 in fidelity.

mics.name: AEA TRP2 (The Ribbon Pre)
mics.description: 2-channel JFET ribbon preamp — 85 dB of quiet, high-impedance gain. Brian's dedicated R88 front end.
mics.summary: The quiet, high-impedance preamp passive ribbons need. 85 dB of clean JFET gain and a 63 kΩ input let the R88 open up. Brian runs it almost exclusively on the R88.
mics.sources: AEA published specifications (TRP2 — The Ribbon Pre); Live Sound KB — classical recording chain
mics.intro: Not a mic — the preamp Brian pairs almost exclusively with the AEA R88. Passive ribbons are quiet and love a high-impedance load, and the TRP2 delivers both: up to 85 dB of clean JFET gain and an extra-high 63 kΩ input impedance that lets the R88's ribbon sound full and open instead of loaded-down and dark. Two channels (perfect for the R88's two ribbons), switchable 100 Hz high-pass and polarity reverse per channel, plus phantom for non-ribbon mics.
mics.sound: Rich and natural with plenty of clean, quiet gain — the high input impedance is the point, opening up the R88's top and dynamics. Use the 100 Hz HPF to tame ribbon proximity; flip polarity to keep the chain aligned.
bestfit: AEA R88 — Brian's near-exclusive pairing; two channels for the two ribbons.
Any passive ribbon (R-121, R-10) needing quiet, high-Z gain.
Low-output sources that need clean gain without noise.
notes: Two channels = a natural fit for the R88's stereo ribbons (Blumlein/MS).
The 63 kΩ input is what makes a passive ribbon sound open rather than dark.
Has phantom on board — but the R88 is passive, so keep 48V OFF for ribbon work.
comparable: Active DI — different job (instruments, not ribbons)

mics.name: Electro-Voice N/D 408
mics.description: Supercardioid N/DYM dynamic — vintage EV tom and guitar-cab mic on a pivoting yoke.
mics.summary: The small-footprint 421 alternative. Supercardioid neodymium dynamic voiced brighter and more aggressive than an SM57, on a pivoting yoke that gets it into tom positions nothing else fits.
mics.sources: Electro-Voice N/D 408B published data sheet (Part No. 531818-201, 1992) — the 408-series acoustic system; Live Sound KB mic-library character notes; live-sound forum consensus (Gearspace, HomeRecording, Tape Op)
mics.photo_source_url: Brian Lloyd — photograph of his own unit, 2026-07-26 (mic is discontinued; no current manufacturer product shot)
mics.intro: A vintage USA-made N/DYM dynamic from the era when Electro-Voice was putting neodymium magnets in everything. Supercardioid, all-metal, and mounted in a pivoting wire yoke that lets the head swing to almost any angle without moving the stand — which is the whole reason it earned its keep on rack toms. The tonal short version: it does the MD 421 job with more upper-mid bite and about a third of the bulk. Brian's is the first-generation N/D 408, no letter suffix, badge confirmed.

specs.Frequency response: 30 Hz – 22 kHz close / 60 Hz – 22 kHz far
specs.Status: Discontinued — superseded by the N/D468 / ND468

mics.sound: Forward and aggressive through the upper mids — brighter than an SM57 and quicker to bite, which is what makes it read on rack toms and medium-gain guitar cabs without help. The published response splits close and far for a reason: worked in tight it reaches to 30 Hz on deliberate proximity, backed off it thins to 60 Hz. Distance is the low-end control on this mic before the HPF is. The supercardioid pattern buys real gain-before-feedback and tight isolation, at the cost of a rear lobe you have to aim around.
bestfit: Rack toms — the reason to own it. The pivoting yoke and small head clear cymbals and the drummer's hands where a 421 clip won't fit.
Guitar cab — more presence and cut than a 57 on medium-gain amps; ease off the top if the amp is already bright.
Snare — brighter crack than a 57, with supercardioid rejection working against the hat.
Horns and loud percussion — handles the SPL; watch the 1–1.5 kHz bark on close brass.
notes: Supercardioid: the null sits around 125°, not 180°. Aim wedges into the null, not straight up the back.
Proximity is voiced in, not a flaw — close response is 30 Hz–22 kHz against 60 Hz–22 kHz far. Set the low end with working distance first, HPF second.
No 48V required. Phantom won't hurt a dynamic, but there's nothing to gain by leaving it on.
Discontinued and vintage — no service parts from EV. The front grille assembly unscrews for cleaning.
Against the MD 421-U: the 421 has more low-mid girth, the 408 more upper-mid bite in a fraction of the space. On a multi-tom kit that's a real reason to split them — 421 on floor, 408 on racks.
The A and B revisions changed the housing and shock mount (N/DYM II and III), not the acoustic system. Brian's plain N/D 408 is the first-generation housing.
comparable: Same jobs with more low-mid weight — and far more bulk
The 408 is brighter and more aggressive through the upper mids
Rack-tom alternative — punchier low-mid lift, less top
The current-production successor; slightly more low-frequency extension
